name: Arabela
confidence_why: Rich 1963 lists several stress patterns for words of the same length and Rich 1999 states outright that Arabela stress is not predictable, Wauters's 2012 field transcriptions mark stress on different syllables with notes that stress moves and depends on the root, and the only dissent, a passing remark in Jiménez 2018 that stress tends to fall on the last syllable of words elicited in isolation, is just what Rich 1963's phrase-final stress rule predicts rather than an analysis of word stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records fixed initial stress; Jiménez says stress tends to be final. This is an aside in a segmental thesis, not a demonstrated analysis, but it is the only explicit placement statement found for this language in the opened sources.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress 'tends to' fall on the last syllable of the word; stated in passing while explaining why vowel-formant averages were not split by stress or position. Stressed vowels are longer (by roughly 0.010-0.040 s) and more peripheral. The thesis is a segmental phonology and has no stress or prosody section; it does not say how stressed syllables were identified.
new_statements.exceptions: 'tiende a' (tends to) only; no exceptions listed. Elsewhere the author suggests /k/ lenition and [ɾ]~[r] variation may be prosodically conditioned (pp. 204, 243) and cites Rich (1999:14) on unstressed vowels being lost between homorganic consonants (p. 226).
new_statements.identity_note: Jiménez 2018 describes the Arabela of the río Arabela (Buena Vista community), Napo district, Maynas, Loreto, based on instrumental recordings of several men and women. Wauters' materials were recorded May-July 2012 in Buena Vista and Santa Clotilde (Napo, Maynas, Loreto) with Edgar Pastor Rosero, Nelly Pastor Rosero and other Rosero-family consultants; same variety, same community. Rich 1975 (SIL) is on the same language but was not opened.

new_statements.quote: Además de los sufijos inflexionales arriba considerados, existen también los que se usan para el imperativo, y que son iguales en forma y sentido a los de arriba, menos en el acento. Frequentamente el acento cae en la penúltima sílaba del predicado imperativo, dejando el sufijo imperative más débil y de pronuncianción corta. Los sufijos imperativos son: -re, -se, -ma, -co, y -rucua, con los mismos alófonos de los sufijos indicativos.
new_statements.translation: Besides the inflectional suffixes considered above, there are also those used for the imperative, which are identical in form and meaning to the ones above, except in the accent. Frequently the accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the imperative predicate, leaving the imperative suffix weaker and short in pronunciation. The imperative suffixes are: -re, -se, -ma, -co, and -rucua, with the same allophones as the indicative suffixes.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2 'StressTyp2', initial stress = fixed initial) records word-initial primary stress. Rich 1975 does not state the general placement, so it neither confirms nor denies initial stress for ordinary words; it adds a morphologically conditioned fact absent from the catalog record: accent distinguishes imperative from indicative predicates, and imperative predicates frequently carry accent on their penultimate syllable. For imperative verb words of three or more syllables that is not initial, so a strictly fixed: initial syllable description would need this as an exception/morphological override. Classed 'refines' (compatible in scope, adds a construction-specific placement)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is a morphosyntactic sketch (valency-changing verbal suffixes, inflectional suffixes, clause types) with no phonology or stress section. Its only statement on accent is construction-specific: imperative and indicative inflectional suffixes are segmentally identical and differ only in accent; in imperative predicates the accent frequently falls on the penultimate syllable of the predicate (the verb word), with the imperative suffix weak and short. No general word-stress rule for non-imperative words is stated, and no claim about tone.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Frequentamente' (frequently) — the penultimate accent in imperatives is given as a tendency, not an exceptionless rule; nothing further.
new_statements.identity_note: Rich 1975 describes Arabela (Zaparoan, Peru) as studied by the author from 1955, data prepared 1960; no dialect distinction is made. Part (B) of the same DEL 18 volume (pp. 18-38) is Thiesen's Bora morphology and is not about Arabela; it was not used.

readall_conflicts: The catalog records fixed initial stress (source StressTyp2). The one explicit placement statement opened, Jiménez 2018 p. 107, says stress 'tends to be located on the last syllable' (final), the opposite edge. Wauters' 2012 field transcriptions (CLA 2016-08, FLEx export) mark stress initially in most 2-3-syllable forms, which supports the catalog against Jiménez for short words, but in 4-5-syllable forms she marks primary stress on the third syllable with a secondary mark on the first, and long-vowel syllables attract the primary mark; her notes say 'stress moves' and 'tone and accent are somewhat variable'. Rich 1975 could not be opened (SIL an automated-access block block), so it neither confirms nor refutes any of these. No direct contradiction from the one work opened: Rich 1975 gives no general word-stress rule, only that imperative predicates 'frequently' take accent on the penultimate syllable of the predicate and that accent alone distinguishes imperative from indicative suffix forms — a morphological accent condition that the StressTyp2 fixed: initial syllable record does not capture and that, for imperative verbs of 3+ syllables, is not initial. Context already held by the project from earlier passes (not in this item's works list, existing_statements empty): Jimenez Peña 2018 (UNMSM thesis, line ~4408, printed p. ~107) remarks in passing that 'el acento tiende a ubicarse en la última sílaba' (stress tends to fall on the last syllable), which is at odds with Stres…

tone.quote: La presente tesis aborda la problemática de las secuencias ambiguas del arabela a nivel segmental, silábico y morfofonológico; sin embargo, no se ahonda en la interacción entre el nivel segmental y los fenómenos prosódicos, tales como el acento, el tono y la entonación. [...] 2.1.1. Rolland Rich y Furne Rich (1961) En este documento inédito, R. Rich y F. Rich exponen un análisis fonológico del nivel segmental, silábico, suprasegmental (acento, entonación y tono) de la lengua arabela.
tone.translation: This thesis addresses the problem of the ambiguous sequences of Arabela at the segmental, syllabic and morphophonological level; however, it does not go into the interaction between the segmental level and prosodic phenomena such as stress, tone and intonation. [...] 2.1.1. Rolland Rich and Furne Rich (1961) In this unpublished document, R. Rich and F. Rich set out a phonological analysis of the segmental, syllabic and suprasegmental (stress, intonation and tone) levels of the Arabela language.

sources.note: Unknown for tone (title/secondary quotations only). It is the fullest first-hand analysis of Arabela word prosody: per Topintzi 2006: 73-75 (quoting it) stress is rhythmic, trochees built left to right, rightmost stress primary, degenerate feet allowed, and 'if a word-final syllable that would have received stress has a voiced onset, and the immediately preceding syllable has a voiceless onset, then the syllable with the voiceless onset is stressed'. Whether it comments on pitch as a stress correlate or on (absence of) tone is not established.
